items.slide_topic: METR time horizon: Mythos at the ceiling of the task suite
items.headline: METR (@METR_Evals) on X, May 8, 2026
items.dek: We evaluated an early version of Claude Mythos Preview for risk assessment during a limited window in March 2026. We estimated a 50%-time-horizon of at least 16hrs (95% CI 8.5hrs to 55hrs) on our task suite, at the upper end of what we can measure without new tasks.

items.slide_topic: METR time horizon: only 5 of 228 tasks are 16h+
items.headline: METR (@METR_Evals) on X, May 8, 2026 (thread 2/5)
items.dek: Of the 228 tasks in our suite, only 5 are estimated as 16+ hours long, making measurements at this range unstable and less meaningful than at ranges with better task coverage. Thus, we are not highlighting exact estimates for models above 16 hours measured with our current suite.

items.headline: METR (@METR_Evals) on X, May 8, 2026 (thread 3/5)
items.dek: We believe that this task suite could still distinguish a much more capable model from current publicly-known state-of-the-art models. But we do not consider measurements at this range to be robust enough for precise quantitative comparisons or extrapolations.

items.slide_topic: METR Frontier Risk Report: TH1.1 'Likely >=16h', MirrorCode 'Mostly saturated'
items.headline: Table 1: There was a modest gap between the internal and public frontier in Feb–Mar 2026 on the evaluations we conducted, though saturation issues make our conclusions highly uncertain.
items.dek: * The TH 1.1 suite can’t reliably measure time horizons above 16 hours, but the 50% time horizon point estimate of the most capable shared model was between 16 and 20 hours, and the 80% time horizon point estimate was between 3 and 4 hours.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Real screenshot of Table 1: TH1.1 50% public ~12h [5h-61h] vs internal 'Likely* >=16h'; Early MirrorCode 'Mostly saturated, >100h time horizon' / 'N/A, due to saturation from public models'; footnote on 16-hour limit
items.notes: Report covers assessment window Feb 16 - Mar 16, 2026; participants Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI.

items.slide_topic: METR: frontier agents 'essentially saturated' the TH1.1 benchmark
items.headline: Coding agents did real projects that would take humans hours or days
items.dek: Benchmarks. The most capable agents we evaluated essentially saturated our Time Horizon 1.1 benchmark — there were only a handful of tasks longer than eight hours that they were still unable to solve, and many of those failures were due to cheating rather than obvious inability. Their measured time horizon was over two full-time-equivalent days, though we are increasingly uncertain about the point estimate due to saturation. Agents displayed even stronger capabilities on an early version of MirrorCode, a software reimplementation benchmark we developed with Epoch AI — the most capable agents we evaluated were able to solve tasks that would take humans weeks.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Real screenshot of the 'Means' section heading + Benchmarks paragraph (strongest single quote on saturation)
items.notes: Footnote 13: MirrorCode result used 'around thirty times as much inference compute as we typically provide to agents on the TH 1.1 suite'.

items.slide_topic: METR: suite saturation makes estimates sensitive to analysis
items.headline: Frontier Risk Report, Appendix E (Time horizon)
items.dek: Recent models have been getting closer to saturating this underlying task suite, which makes the estimated time horizon less constrained by the data and more sensitive to analysis decisions.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Real screenshot of the Appendix E paragraph

items.slide_topic: METR: 'infeasible to precisely measure' above 16 h
items.headline: Frontier Risk Report, Appendix E (Time horizon)
items.dek: The best measured 50% time horizon of any shared model was lower than 20 hours, although since only 5 tasks in the TH1.1 suite are estimated to take humans longer than 16 hours, it is infeasible to precisely measure time horizons in this range. We therefore cannot say with confidence that the “true” time horizon is under 20 hours.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Real screenshot of the Appendix E paragraph

items.slide_topic: New longer tasks: MirrorCode horizons far above TH1.1
items.headline: For public models as of Feb–Mar 2026, MirrorCode-Early time horizons were higher than on our Time Horizon 1.1 suite
items.dek: Figure 4: We find that public models in Feb–Mar 2026 had several times longer time horizons on the software reimplementation tasks in MirrorCode-Early than they did on the broader Time Horizon 1.1 suite. While we have limited data, the doubling time seems similar or slightly faster. The MirrorCode agents had different token limits, which could lead to overestimating the doubling time, see details in Appendix E.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Original METR CC-BY chart (1647x947): MirrorCode tasks (pink, doubling 82 days, top point ~128h+) vs TH1.1 tasks (green, doubling 105 days), log scale to 256h
items.notes: Page: https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-19-frontier-risk-report/ . MirrorCode used ~30x the inference compute of TH1.1 runs (footnote 13).

items.slide_topic: GPT-5.6 Sol: estimate 'well beyond the range' the suite can measure
items.headline: Summary of METR's predeployment evaluation of GPT-5.6 Sol
items.dek: With the data we collected for GPT-5.6 Sol, if we follow our standard methodology of marking cheating attempts as failures, we arrive at a 50%-Time Horizon point estimate of around 11.3hrs (95% CI: 5hrs - 40hrs), but if we count the cheating attempts as legitimate successes, the point estimate jumps beyond 270hrs – well beyond the range where we consider our task suite to give reliable measurements. Discarding the cheating attempts leaves us with no data for several informative long-horizon tasks, and results in a highly uncertain point estimate of 71hrs (95% CI: 13hrs - 11400hrs). This makes us especially uncertain about the time-horizon measurement, and we do not consider any of these numbers to represent a robust measurement of GPT-5.6 Sol’s capabilities.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Real screenshot of the key paragraph (11.3h vs 71h vs >270h depending on how cheating is scored)
items.notes: Same post: 'GPT-5.6 Sol’s detected cheating rate was higher than any public model we have evaluated on our ReAct agent harness.' METR still judged Sol 'not significantly beyond the state-of-the-art'. Post was reviewed/approved by OpenAI comms+legal (stated in post).

items.slide_topic: METR: working on raising the ceiling (Jan 2026)
items.headline: We are working on raising the ceiling of our capabilities measurements.
items.dek: As discussed above, even our Time Horizon 1.1 suite has relatively few tasks that the latest generation of models cannot perform successfully. We are prioritizing work on updates to our evaluations so they can measure the capabilities of very strong models.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Real screenshot from the Time Horizon 1.1 release post
items.notes: Same post: 'These confidence intervals are still very wide, and we are actively working on adding more long tasks to help get tighter estimates and avoid saturation as model capabilities continue to advance.' TH1.1 went from 170 to 228 tasks; 8h+ tasks from 14 to 31.

items.slide_topic: METR note: as the suite saturates, results become sensitive
items.headline: Impact of modeling assumptions on time horizon results
items.dek: As METR’s time horizon task suite saturates, the results are becoming more sensitive to analysis choices. One example of this was the recent update to fix a modeling mistake with regularization, which decreased recent models’ 50% time horizon results by up to 20%, but had a smaller impact on earlier LLMs’ 50% time horizons.
items.author: Alexander Barry
items.caption: Real screenshot of the note's opening paragraph
items.notes: Same note: 'the TH1.1 task suite does not contain any very long (>30 hour) tasks, and so the right hand tail of the curve is not meaningfully constrained.'

items.slide_topic: METR note: benchmark begins to saturate (Jan 2026)
items.headline: Clarifying limitations of time horizon
items.dek: Error bars have historically been a factor of ~2 in each direction, worse with current models like Opus 4.5 as our benchmark begins to saturate.
items.author: Thomas Kwa
items.caption: Real screenshot of one bullet
items.notes: Same note: 'I still think it’s fine but have increasing worries as the benchmark nears saturation.'

items.slide_topic: New longer tasks: MirrorCode (weeks-long tasks)
items.headline: METR (@METR_Evals) on X, Apr 10, 2026
items.dek: We co-developed MirrorCode with @EpochAIResearch to test AI on extremely long-horizon blackbox software reimplementation tasks. We found that recent public models are able to fully implement at least some programs we estimate would take humans weeks or months to implement. | Notably, these are much longer than what we’ve measured on Time Horizon 1.1 (our standard agentic task suite). This could be because these tasks provide a precise, checkable specification, and/or because AI companies are already training on similar tasks.
items.author: METR
items.caption: Real screenshot of METR quote-tweet of Epoch AI (with Epoch's MirrorCode chart: Opus 4.6 passes 7,700-LoC 'gotree'; 'Pkl' hits 1B token limit) plus METR's follow-up reply
items.notes: Reply URL: https://x.com/METR_Evals/status/2042666178540429698 . Embedded Epoch tweet text: 'In our new benchmark, MirrorCode, Claude Opus 4.6 reimplemented a 16,000-line bioinformatics toolkit — a task we believe would take a human engineer weeks.'

facts.claim: METR: Claude Mythos Preview (early) has a 50% time horizon of 'at least 16hrs (95% CI 8.5hrs to 55hrs) … at the upper end of what we can measure without new tasks.'

METR's dashboard reads 'Predicted 50% time horizon: 17 hr' for Claude Mythos Preview (early) — with the notice 'Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite' (raw estimate 17.4 h).
facts.source: METR, Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models

facts.claim: Of the 228 tasks in METR's suite, only 5 are estimated to take humans 16+ hours — so METR is 'not highlighting exact estimates for models above 16 hours'.
METR: 'we do not consider measurements at this range to be robust enough for precise quantitative comparisons or extrapolations.'

METR: measuring stronger models requires 'adding longer tasks, and we’re working on updated methods. But these are still in development; for now, we advise caution in interpreting recent time-horizon numbers.'

METR: 'The most capable agents we evaluated essentially saturated our Time Horizon 1.1 benchmark — there were only a handful of tasks longer than eight hours that they were still unable to solve, and many of those failures were due to cheating rather than obvious inability.'
facts.source: METR, Frontier Risk Report (February to March 2026)

facts.claim: METR: 'The TH 1.1 suite can’t reliably measure time horizons above 16 hours' — the best internal model shared with METR (Feb–Mar 2026) scored between 16 and 20 hours; METR 'cannot say with confidence that the “true” time horizon is under 20 hours.'

On METR/Epoch's longer MirrorCode tasks, public frontier models were already 'Mostly saturated, >100h time horizon' (Feb–Mar 2026); agents solved tasks 'that would take humans weeks' (using ~30x the usual inference compute).
facts.source: METR, Frontier Risk Report, Table 1 + footnote 13

facts.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol: METR's time-horizon estimate swings from ~11.3 h to 71 h to 'beyond 270hrs – well beyond the range where we consider our task suite to give reliable measurements', depending on how cheating runs are scored.
facts.source: METR, GPT-5.6 Sol predeployment evaluation summary

facts.claim: METR (Jan 2026): 'even our Time Horizon 1.1 suite has relatively few tasks that the latest generation of models cannot perform successfully. We are prioritizing work on updates to our evaluations so they can measure the capabilities of very strong models.'
METR's time-horizon suite tops out at a single 30-hour task; only 5 of 228 tasks exceed 16 hours (31 exceed 8 hours).
facts.source: METR task_results_1_1.yaml (raw data) + METR TH1.1 post

facts.claim: Cheating clusters at the ceiling: for TH1.1 tasks over 8 hours, 'at least 16% of successful runs were illegitimate upon review.'
As of 2026-10-04 METR's time-horizon dashboard is still 'LAST UPDATED May 8, 2026'; it lists Claude Opus 4.7, Grok 4.3 and GPT-5.5 among 'recent models that don’t currently have time horizons'.
facts.source: METR, Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models
